fields.meta_title: One Page Website Builder With a Working Form | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a one page website from one prompt: sections in scroll order and a form that saves every inquiry to your database. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a One Page Website With a Form That Works
fields.hero_description: Describe the business and the sections it needs. Emergent builds the one page website with menu links that jump to each section, plus a form that saves to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: The Parts of a One Page Website Emergent Builds
fields.features_subheading: Each part comes from your prompt, and each one changes with a follow-up message.
fields.feature_1:
Sections in the order visitors scroll

Emergent lays out the intro, services, reviews and contact sections in the order your prompt lists them. Adding a section later means naming it and saying where it should sit.
fields.feature_2:
Menu links that jump down the page

Every section gets an anchor, and each header link scrolls to its section. Ask for a pinned header and it stays in view on a phone, with the menu folded into one button.
fields.feature_3:
Every inquiry saved as a row

Inquiries are saved to a database you own, one row per submission, with the fields your prompt names. A new entry can also post to Slack or email whoever answers it.
fields.feature_4:
Edits made by message, not by dragging

Send a message such as "move reviews above pricing" or "add a second phone number to the footer," and Emergent rewrites that part of the code. Nothing is dragged into place.
fields.feature_5:
Live on a domain with your name on it

Your page goes live on a custom domain, which Emergent includes and bills in credits. Publishing also works on the free tier, before you have bought a domain name at all.
fields.feature_6:
Code you can take anywhere

Nothing stays locked in Emergent. Export the full code, contact form included, to your GitHub repository, where a developer can host it on their own server or extend it.

fields.usecase_heading: One Page Websites for Four Trades
fields.tab_content_1:
Portfolio first, inquiry form last, one scroll

Dana Reyes shoots products and portraits for small brands. Her page opens on a grid of recent shoots and ends with an inquiry form asking for the shoot date and budget, with her packages in between. Each inquiry is saved to a table, and any budget of $2,500 or more posts to her Slack.
fields.tab_content_2:
Every quote request checked against the service area

Plumbing calls come from the towns Harbor Lane Plumbing covers, and a few from places it does not. The page puts the phone number in the header and a quote form at the bottom. Requests from a town outside the service area are tagged Out of area before anyone calls back.
fields.tab_content_3:
Large parties go to the events manager

The reservation form sits under Juniper Table's menu. Parties of 8 or fewer go straight into the bookings table. A request for 10 guests skips the table: Lena, the events manager, gets it by email with the party size and the requested time.
fields.tab_content_4:
When the race fills, signups become a waitlist

At 400 runners, the Riverside 5K page stops taking registrations. The course map and race-morning schedule stay up, and the signup button opens a waitlist form instead. Each entry gets a numbered spot and a confirmation email with that number.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a One Page Website
fields.howto_description: Start with the one thing a visitor should do, then build every section toward it. The form at the bottom is where the page earns its keep.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Check that one page is enough
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 List the sections in scroll order
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Describe the page in one prompt
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Link the menu to each section
fields.howto_step_1_des: A one-page site fits a business with one offer and one action a visitor should take, such as booking a table or asking for a quote. If you sell unrelated services to different buyers, give each of them a page of its own.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Write the sections down in the order a visitor needs them: what you do, proof that you do it well, what it costs, how to reach you. Cut any section that repeats another, and keep the contact form as the last stop.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Name the business, the sections and the details only you know: phone number, service towns, package prices, opening hours. Emergent builds the first version from that prompt. The more specific the details, the less copy you rewrite afterward.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Ask for a header menu whose links jump to each section, and give sections short names that match those links. Keep the menu to the sections visitors look for first; four or five links fit on a phone screen.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Pick the fields the form asks for and what happens to each entry: a row in your database, an email to you, a Slack post for the large jobs. Ask only for fields you will use when you reply to someone.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Test the scroll on a phone
fields.howto_step_6_des: Open the page on your own phone and scroll it end to end. Tap every menu link, submit the form once and confirm the entry landed where you asked. Describe anything awkward in a message and Emergent fixes it.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Publish the page and connect the domain you bought. Then put the link wherever customers already look for you: your Google Business Profile and Instagram bio first, then the email signature on every reply you send.

plan.angle: The top 10 is galleries (One Page Love, Awwwards, Made in Webflow), template shops (Nicepage, Etsy, Webflow templates) and builder blogs (Wix, Squarespace, Framer). They show what a one-pager looks like; none shows what happens after a visitor fills in its form. This page wins by covering when one page is enough, the sections in scroll order, and four real businesses whose one action (inquire, request a quote, reserve, register) lands in a database the owner keeps, with Emergent as the builder that hands over the code.

Juniper Table's menu page takes reservations for parties of 8 or fewer straight into its bookings table and sends a party of 10 to the events manager.
A Riverside 5K page stops registration at 400 runners and turns its signup button into a waitlist form that numbers each new entry.
